data.title: Alopecia areata — viva
data.summary: Hair & nail disorders · 30 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Alopecia areata** (Hair & nail disorders)_

**Q1. Define alopecia areata (AA).**
- Chronic, relapsing, immune-mediated, non-scarring hair loss with well-circumscribed patches of hair loss on scalp or any hair-bearing area, with preserved follicular openings; affects ~2% lifetime; any age, peak 20–40 y

**Q2. Classify alopecias (PYQ).**
- Non-scarring (non-cicatricial): AA, androgenetic alopecia, telogen effluvium, anagen effluvium, trichotillomania, traction (early), tinea capitis (non-inflammatory), secondary syphilis, hair shaft defects, hypothyroidism, nutritional
- Scarring (cicatricial) — primary: lymphocytic (DLE, LPP, frontal fibrosing alopecia, central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia, pseudopelade of Brocq), neutrophilic (folliculitis decalvans, dissecting cellulitis), mixed (acne keloidalis, erosive pustular dermatosis); secondary: burns, radiation, trauma, kerion, tumours, morphoea, infections (lupus vulgaris)

**Q3. Describe the hair cycle (PYQ).**
- Anagen (growth): 2–7 years, ~85–90% of scalp hairs, determines length
- Catagen (regression): 2–3 weeks, ~1%
- Telogen (rest): ~3 months, 10–15%; club hair shed in exogen
- Kenogen: empty follicle interval; scalp has ~100,000 hairs, normal shedding 50–100/day; growth ~1 cm/month

**Q4. Pathogenesis of AA.**
- Collapse of immune privilege of anagen hair bulb (reduced MHC I, TGF-β, α-MSH) → autoreactive CD8+NKG2D+ T cells attack follicular autoantigens (melanocyte/keratinocyte), IFN-γ and IL-15 via JAK–STAT signalling → follicle forced into dystrophic anagen/telogen; follicle stem cells spared (non-scarring, reversible)
- Genetic (HLA-DQB1, ULBP, CTLA4, IL2RA), family history 10–20%, stress, viral infections, vaccination triggers
- Associations: atopy, thyroid autoimmunity, vitiligo, Down syndrome, APECED, lupus, diabetes, iron deficiency

**Q5. Clinical patterns and signs.**
- Patchy (commonest), ophiasis (band along occipital and temporal margins — poor prognosis), sisaipho (inverse ophiasis — frontoparietal), diffuse (acute diffuse and total alopecia — mimics TE), alopecia totalis (whole scalp), universalis (all body hair), reticular
- Exclamation-mark hairs (tapering proximal ends) at active edge, positive pull test at margin, regrowth with white (vellus) hairs first, sparing of grey hairs ('sudden whitening overnight')
- Nails (10–60%): fine regular geometric pitting, trachyonychia, Beau's lines, red lunulae, onychomadesis

**Q6. Trichoscopy in AA.**
- Yellow dots (keratin in empty follicles), black dots (cadaverised hairs — active), exclamation-mark hairs, broken hairs, tapered hairs, short vellus/regrowing hairs, Pohl–Pinkus constrictions

**Q7. Histopathology.**
- Peribulbar lymphocytic infiltrate ('swarm of bees') around anagen bulbs (acute), increased catagen/telogen hairs, miniaturised follicles, fibrous streamers, pigment casts, eosinophils; no scarring

**Q8. Severity assessment.**
- SALT score (Severity of Alopecia Tool): % scalp hair loss — vertex 40%, posterior 24%, each side 18% — S1 <25%, S2 25–49, S3 50–74, S4 75–99, S5 100%; severe AA = SALT ≥50
- Alopecia areata investigator global assessment (AA-IGA)

**Q9. Differential diagnosis.**
- Tinea capitis (scaling, broken hairs, KOH), trichotillomania (bizarre shapes, broken hairs of varying length, no exclamation-mark hairs, trichoscopy — flame hairs, tulip hairs, V-sign), telogen effluvium (diffuse, positive pull test everywhere), secondary syphilis (moth-eaten), androgenetic alopecia (diffuse AA), early scarring alopecia, traction alopecia, loose anagen syndrome, temporal triangular alopecia (congenital)

**Q10. Investigations.**
- Clinical/trichoscopy; thyroid function and antibodies, CBC, ferritin, vitamin D, blood sugar; VDRL if moth-eaten; KOH; biopsy if doubtful

**Q11. Treatment.**
- Limited patchy (<50%): intralesional triamcinolone acetonide 2.5–10 mg/ml (5 mg/ml commonly) every 4–6 weeks (first line in adults), super-potent topical steroids (children), minoxidil 5% adjunct, topical immunotherapy for chronic (DPCP, SADBE — induce allergic contact dermatitis), anthralin short contact (children)
- Extensive/rapidly progressive: oral mini-pulse betamethasone/dexamethasone 5 mg twice weekly, pulse methylprednisolone, short oral prednisolone; methotrexate (± low-dose steroid), azathioprine, cyclosporine, oral minoxidil
- JAK inhibitors for severe AA (SALT ≥50): baricitinib 4 mg (FDA 2022, adults; approved in India), ritlecitinib 50 mg (≥12 y), deuruxolitinib; tofacitinib off-label — monitor CBC, lipids, LFT, infections (TB/HZV screening)
- Supportive: wigs, hair pieces, eyebrow tattooing/microblading, counselling, support groups

**Q12. Prognosis.**
- ~50% of limited patchy AA regrow within a year without treatment; poor prognostic factors — onset in childhood, extensive (totalis/universalis), ophiasis, long duration (>1 y), nail changes, atopy, family history, associated autoimmunity, Down syndrome

**Q13. What is immune privilege of the hair follicle and its collapse?**
- Anagen bulb normally has low MHC class I, local immunosuppressants (TGF-β, α-MSH, IL-10, CGRP) — protecting follicle autoantigens
- In AA, IFN-γ (and stressors/ viral triggers) upregulates MHC class I/II, NKG2D ligands (MICA, ULBP3) → CD8+ NKG2D+ T cells attack the bulb → dystrophic anagen/ catagen; IFN-γ–JAK1/2 and IL-15–JAK1/3 signalling (rationale for JAK inhibitors)

**Q14. Describe the exclamation-mark hair and other signs.**
- Exclamation-mark hair: short broken hair, thicker distally and tapering proximally with depigmented root — sign of active disease (at the edge of patches)
- Positive hair-pull test at margin (active), Coudability sign (hairs bend at the base), cadaver hairs/ black dots, regrowth of white (vellus) hairs first
- Sudden whitening ('turning white overnight') — selective loss of pigmented hairs

**Q15. Describe the clinical patterns.**
- Patchy (commonest), multifocal, reticular, ophiasis (band along occipital and temporal margins — poor prognosis), sisaipho (ophiasis inversus — frontoparietal), diffuse AA (mimics TE), alopecia totalis (whole scalp), universalis (all body hair), AA incognita (diffuse thinning with yellow dots), beard/ eyebrow/ eyelash AA

**Q16. Associated conditions.**
- Atopy (eczema, asthma — poorer prognosis), thyroid autoimmunity, vitiligo, type 1 diabetes, coeliac disease, lupus, Down syndrome (higher prevalence), autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1 (APECED), psychiatric stress, iron/ vitamin D deficiency

**Q17. Nail changes in AA.**
- Fine regular geometric pitting ('Scotch plaid'), trachyonychia, longitudinal ridging, red/ mottled lunulae, onychomadesis — more common in severe AA (marker of poor prognosis)

**Q18. How is SALT score calculated?**
- Severity of Alopecia Tool: scalp divided — vertex 40%, right side 18%, left side 18%, posterior 24%; % hair loss in each area × its weight summed (0–100); S1 25–49%, S2 25–49 ... (S0 no loss, S1 <25%, S2 25–49%, S3 50–74%, S4a 75–95%, S4b 96–99%, S5 100%); SALT ≤20 used as response target in trials

**Q19. Intralesional steroid therapy — practical points.**
- Triamcinolone acetonide 2.5–10 mg/ml (5 mg/ml commonly on scalp, 2.5 mg/ml on face/eyebrows), 0.05–0.1 ml per injection point 1 cm apart into deep dermis, every 4–6 weeks; maximum ~20 mg per session; side effects — atrophy (reversible), hypopigmentation, telangiectasia; best for limited patchy AA (<50% scalp) in adults

**Q20. Topical immunotherapy — mechanism and protocol.**
- Induces allergic contact dermatitis with diphenylcyclopropenone (DPCP) or squaric acid dibutyl ester (SADBE) — antigenic competition shifts the immune response away from the follicle ('perifollicular CD4/CD8 ratio change')
- Sensitise with 2% on a small area, then weekly applications starting 0.001% and increasing until mild eczema persists 24–36 h; continue 12–24 weeks; response ~50–60% in extensive AA; side effects — severe eczema, lymphadenopathy, pigment changes (vitiligo/ dyschromia in confetti), urticaria

**Q21. Systemic steroids in AA — regimens.**
- Oral mini-pulse: betamethasone/dexamethasone 5 mg on two consecutive days weekly for 3–6 months
- Monthly pulses (prednisolone 300 mg or methylprednisolone 500 mg × 3 days), short courses of prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg tapering — relapse common on stopping; use for rapidly progressive disease

**Q22. JAK inhibitors in AA — details.**
- Baricitinib (JAK1/2) 2–4 mg/day — approved for severe AA (≥50% SALT) in adults; ritlecitinib (JAK3/ TEC) 50 mg/day — approved ≥12 y; deuruxolitinib (JAK1/2) approved in US; tofacitinib off-label (cheaper — widely used in India)
- Response: SALT ≤20 in ~35–40% at 36 weeks, better with longer duration; eyebrow/eyelash regrowth; relapse after stopping
- Monitoring: TB, hepatitis, CBC, lipids, LFT, CK; risks — infections, acne, VTE, MACE in older smokers

**Q23. Other treatments.**
- Topical minoxidil 5% (adjunct), anthralin short-contact (irritant therapy), topical steroids (children), methotrexate (± steroids), cyclosporine, azathioprine, simvastatin/ezetimibe (weak), excimer laser, PRP, low-level laser; hairpieces/ wigs, eyebrow tattooing/ microblading, psychological support
- Children: topical steroids, minoxidil, anthralin, DPCP (older children), mini-pulse steroids for extensive progressive disease

**Q24. Poor prognostic factors in AA.**
- Onset in childhood, long duration (>1 year), extensive loss (totalis/universalis), ophiasis pattern, nail involvement, atopy, family history, associated autoimmunity, Down syndrome, multiple relapses

**Q25. Differentiate AA from tinea capitis and trichotillomania.**
- Tinea capitis: scaling, inflammation, broken hairs, black dots, comma/corkscrew hairs on trichoscopy, KOH positive
- Trichotillomania: irregular patches with hairs of varying lengths, no exclamation-mark hairs, broken hairs with trichoptilosis, V-sign, flame hairs on trichoscopy, behavioural history
- AA: smooth patch, exclamation-mark hairs, yellow dots, regrowing vellus hairs

**Q26. What psychiatric issues are linked and how to address?**
- Anxiety, depression, social phobia, low self-esteem; validated QoL tools (AA-QLI, Skindex); offer counselling, support groups, camouflage; screen children for bullying

**Q27. What is the role of vitamin D and iron in AA?**
- Low serum vitamin D and ferritin are frequently reported in AA; correct deficiencies (not proven as primary treatment); topical calcipotriol has modest benefit in patchy AA

**Q28. Histopathology of AA by stage.**
- Acute: peribulbar 'swarm of bees' lymphocytic infiltrate around anagen bulbs, eosinophils, pigment incontinence
- Subacute: increased catagen/telogen hairs
- Chronic: miniaturised follicles, fibrous streamers, reduced terminal:vellus ratio, minimal inflammation; no scarring — follicles preserved

**Q29. Differential diagnosis of diffuse AA.**
- Telogen effluvium (normal trichoscopy, club hairs), androgenetic alopecia (miniaturisation pattern, no exclamation hairs), anagen effluvium (chemotherapy), syphilitic alopecia (moth-eaten), SLE alopecia, loose anagen syndrome (children — ruffled cuticle, painless pluckable hairs)

**Q30. Prognosis in patchy AA.**
- Most limited patchy AA regrow within 1 year (spontaneous regrowth in ~50%); relapses common (~85% have more than one episode); ~5–10% progress to totalis/universalis

## Quick spotter facts
- Smooth round patch with exclamation-mark hairs — AA
- Yellow dots, black dots on trichoscopy
- Severe AA — baricitinib/ritlecitinib

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Alopecia areata); SALT score; JAK inhibitor approvals. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
